Pediatric stiff limb syndrome with polyautoimmunity of anti-GAD-65, 
anti-islet cell, and thyroid peroxidase antibodies: A case report and review 
of literature

ABSTRACT  
We report an early childhood onset Stiff Limb Syndrome (SLS) in association with unusual polyautoimmunity of 
GAD-65, anti-islet cell, and Thyroid Peroxidase (TPO) autoantibodies, who has achieved a nearly complete 
neurological recovery following combined immunotherapy, symptomatic and physical therapy. The patient had 
normal MRIs of the brain and spinal cord and a negative paraneoplastic work-up. Subsequently, she developed 
hypothyroidism requiring levothyroxine supplementation. We then conducted an extensive review of literature 
and identified 52 previously reported pediatric Stiff Man Syndrome (SMS)/Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS) or SLS 
cases, which has demonstrated a common association with other systemic autoimmune conditions. In the 
available literature, screening for concurrent autoimmunity has only been reported infrequently. We found that a 
paraneoplastic process is extremely rare in pediatric cases. Timely diagnosis and initiation of immunotherapy are 
critical to a favorable outcome. Therefore, we recommend to include SMS/SPS or SLS as an important differential 
diagnosis for MRI-negative myelopathy. Further clinical and research efforts should be focused on understanding 
the role of both genetic predisposition and environmental insults in the autoimmunity of pediatric SMS/SPS or 
SLS.   
1. Introduction 
Stiff Man Syndrome (SMS)/Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS) and its 
variant Stiff Limb Syndrome (SLS) are rare autoimmune neurological 
disorders frequently associated with the presence of serum and/or ce -
rebrospinal fluid (CSF) anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) 
and/or anti-glycine receptor (anti-GlyR) antibodies. The disease mani -
fests across a wide clinical spectrum including painful spasms, hyper -
reflexia, axial rigidity, lower extremity rigidity or spasticity, gait 
abnormalities, and hyperlordosis ( Yeshokumar et al., 2021 ). The disease 
was previously classified into classical SMS/SPS, SLS, and progressive 
encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) ( Hadavi et al., 
2011 ). In addition, SMS/SPS is strongly associated with other 
autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), auto -
immune thyroid disease, and connective tissue disorders. Although in a

small subset of adult patients SMS/SPS presented in a paraneoplastic 
context ( McKeon et al., 2012 ), this association remains uncertain in 
children diagnosed with SMS/SPS or SLS. 
Here we describe an early childhood onset case of SLS that was 
associated with high titers of anti-GAD-65 antibodies in the serum and 
CSF, as well as abnormally elevated serum anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA), 
anti-islet cell and thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies. The child had a 
negative paraneoplastic work-up and achieved nearly full recovery with 
immunotherapy, symptomatic and physical therapy. She subsequently 
developed autoimmune thyroiditis requiring levothyroxine supplemen -
tation. She has been closely monitored for development of T1DM.

2. Methods 
An extensive literature search for pediatric onset SMS/SPS or SLS 
was conducted. We searched databases including PubMed, EMBASE, 
and Web of Science for publications, using searching terms “ Stiff man 
syndrome ” or “ Stiff person syndrome ” or “ Stiff limb syndrome ” . The 
Boolean ‘AND ’ was used to combine these terms with “ pediatric ” or 
“ child ” or “ childhood ” . A total 406 abstracts were screened after 
removal of 126 duplicates. Exclusion criteria were as follows: 1) lack of a 
diagnosis of SMS/SPS or SLS; 2) duplicate cases previously published; 3) 
lack of clinical details such as age, sex, neurological syndrome, etiology, 
comorbidities, treatment received and outcome. 367 records were 
excluded. We then reviewed 39 full text articles and further excluded 
articles that were published in languages other than English or before 
1980, or cases with onset age older than 18 years. 28 articles were 
included in this literature review ( Fig. 1 ). 
3. Case presentation 
An 18-month-old ex-full-term developmentally typical female with 
congenital first-degree AV block and tricuspid regurgitation presented to 
the emergency department (ED) due to inability to bear weight in her 
right lower extremity. Approximately 10 days prior to her hospital visit, 
her mother noted that she had a ‘wobbly gait ’ and a pain probably 
localized to her right hip that progressed over two days to no longer 
being able to ambulate and she preferred to crawl while dragging her leg 
behind her. There was no known trauma or injury. Parents endorsed a 
common cold approximately three weeks prior. She initially presented 
to an urgent care and then her pediatrician ’ s office where work-up 
included plain films of the right foot, fibula and tibia, all of which 
were normal. Laboratory data including a complete blood count, sedi -
mentation rate, C-reactive protein, Lyme titers and blood cultures were 
remarkable only for thrombocytosis to 659,000/mcl and leukocytosis to 
15,500/mcl. Symptoms continued to progress and the patient was 
referred back to the ED. On arrival , she was afebrile and hemody -
namically stable. Initially a musculoskeletal cause for her symptoms was 
pursued by the orthopedic team including repeat X-rays of the right 
tibia, fibula, femur, foot, pelvis and hips, all of which were normal. 
Repeat laboratory testing was also unremarkable aside from an elevated 
platelet count to 497,000/mcl; her leukocytosis had resolved. Magnetic 
resonance imaging (MRI) of the right hip and ankle was pursued and was 
normal. The patient was eventually discharged with possible diagnoses 
of transient synovitis or reactive arthritis of the hip or ankle. 
The patient presented again to the hospital 9 days later with 
continued functional decline. At that point she was unable to sit up 
without being assisted. Mother denied bowel or bladder dysfunction. On 
this admission neurology was consulted. Her initial neurologic exam 
was notable for rigidity, hypertonia and hyperreflexia on the right lower 
extremity compared to the left. Her interphalangeal (IP) joints of the big 
toes were in over-flexion. There was also reduced passive range of mo -
tion (ROM) in dorsiflexion and plantar flexion of both ankles, right more 
prominent than left. MRI of the entire neuro-axis was performed and was 
unremarkable. A lumbar puncture (LP) was pursued and the CSF routine

analysis was also normal (glucose 42, protein 17, RBCs 0 and nucleated 
cells 2). CSF neurotransmitters ( MNG lab ) and the gene panel for 
neurotransmitter disorders ( Invitae ) were sent and returned later as 
negative. Serum amino acids (SAA), urine organic acids (UOA) and CSF 
amino acids were unremarkable. She had also negative Lyme titer twice, 
normal creatinine kinase, acylcarnitine profile, serum copper and 
ceruloplasmin levels. At this point a search for more rare causes of MRI- 
negative myelopathy was pursued including both a serum and CSF 
screening for autoimmune myelopathy ( Mayo Clinic lab ). Notably, dur -
ing this time anti-ANA titers were abnormally elevated at 1:1,280 
(speckled). Anti-TPO antibodies were also elevated at 505 IU/ML and 
anti-islet cell antibodies elevated at 1,280 JDF units ( Table 1 ). There was 
consideration of empiric glucocorticoids treatment at that time. It was 
put on hold due to a worry for steroid-induced hyperglycemia, given her 
risk for T1DM, plus her symptoms began to slowly improve with 
intensive physical therapy. She was discharged with a close outpatient 
follow-up while awaiting autoimmune myelopathy panels to result. 
Soon after discharge the CSF autoimmune panel revealed an abnor -
mally elevated anti-GAD-65 antibodies at 4.79 nmol/l, with negative 
amphiphysin antibodies and negative NMO/AQP4 IgG levels. Serum 
anti-GAD-65 antibodies were remarkably elevated at 396 nmol/l (ref <
0.02 nmol/l) ( Table 1 ). This confirmed a diagnosis of SLS with positive 
anti-GAD-65 antibodies. Electromyography (EMG)/nerve conduction 
study was cancelled. She was subsequently started on a low dose of 
diazepam (2.5 mg by mouth three times a day) for spasticity and was 
then admitted for intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) treatment. Diaz -
epam was soon switched to clonazepam 0.25 mg by mouth twice daily 
after difficulty sleeping, decreased appetite, and loose stools were re -
ported as side-effects on diazepam. 
The patient continued to improve clinically over the next few weeks. 
She followed up with pediatric endocrinology and her linear growth was 
noted to be appropriate for her genetic potential. She had a work-up for 
endocrine conditions that included anti-insulin antibodies, insulin-like 
growth factor-1 (IGF-1), IGF binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3), cortisol, ad -
renocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), thyroid stimulating hormone 
(TSH), free T4, and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c). Her HbA1c was normal, 
ruling out T1DM, but her anti-insulin antibodies were positive, consis -
tent with the positive anti-GAD-65 and anti-islet cell antibodies and 
indicating an increased risk for developing T1DM. IGF-1 was low for age, 
IGFBP-3 was normal; cortisol and ACTH were normal, ruling out adrenal 
insufficiency, and TSH and free T4 were normal, consistent with 
euthyroid Hashimoto ’ s thyroiditis. Evaluation for other systemic auto -
immune diseases was pursued including anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, anti- 
RNP, anti-SSA, anti-SSB, and centromere B antibodies, anti-beta2 
glycoprotein IgG and IgM, anti-cardiolipin IgG, IgM, and IgA anti -
bodies, lupus anti-coagulant, tissue transglutaminase IgA, and results 
were all reassuring. A whole-body PET/CT (positron emission tomog -
raphy/computed tomography) scan showed no evidence of fluo -
rodeoxyglucose (FDG) avid malignancy. 
After receiving two treatments of monthly IVIG infusion (each 
treatment consisting of 1,000 mg/kg/day for two consecutive days), the

repeat serum anti-GAD-65 level was down-trending to 284. Given 
drastic clinical improvement, IVIG was temporally paused following the

3rd infusion. However, after a 2-month pause the titers of GAD-65, TPO 
and ANA antibodies had rebounded ( Table 1 ). Therefore, IVIG infusion 
had been resumed. Eight months after initial presentation, the patient 
developed autoimmune hypothyroidism and treatment with levothyr -
oxine was started. Patient followed with pediatric cardiology regularly 
and had stable cardiac status throughout the course. The Invitae primary 
immunodeficiency panel (407 genes) was non-diagnostic but revealed 
several heterozygous variants of unknown significance (VUS) in C2 
( c .259G > C; p. Val87Leu), CIITA ( c .2342C > G; p .Ser781Trp), NLRP12 
( c. 1790G > A; p. Ser597Asn), SAMD9L ( c. 982 T > C; p. Cys328Arg), and 
SRP72 ( c. 803A > G; p. Asn268Ser) genes. Of note, NLRP12, SAMD9L, 
and SRP72 genes are associated with autosomal dominant conditions, 
which are familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, ataxia- 
pancytopenia (AP) syndrome, and familial bone marrow failure, 
respectively. Parental study and whole exosome sequencing (WES) were 
recommended in a continued search for a genetic predisposition. 
4. Discussion 
The patient described above was an 18-month-old child who pre -
sented with polyautoimmunity of anti-GAD-65, anti-Islet cell, anti- 
insulin, and TPO antibodies that led to a clinical manifestation of SLS 
and subsequent autoimmune hypothyroidism. She is euglycemic so far, 
as demonstrated by her normal HbA1c; however, positive anti-islet cell 
and anti-insulin antibodies, together with the anti-GAD-65 antibodies 
render an increased risk of developing T1DM to around 84% by the time 
she is 18 years old ( DiMeglio et al., 2018 ). Based on the literature re -
view, this is the first case of pediatric onset SMS/SPS or SLS who has 
demonstrated the laboratory evidence of polyautoimmunity. 
GAD-65 is the rate-limiting enzyme in the synthesis of gamma- 
aminobutyric acid (GABA), an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the cen -
tral nervous system (CNS) and pancreatic beta cells. GAD-65 autoanti -
bodies are detected in 80% of patients with newly diagnosed T1DM; but 
the titer of anti-GAD Ab is much higher (around 50 – 100-fold) in SMS/ 
SPS than in T1DM. The Mayo clinic has established a normal range for 
serum GAD-65 antibody at 0.00 – 0.02 nmol/l using immunoprecipita -
tion assay (IPA). Values greater than 100 nmol/l are strongly associated 
with various neurological phenotypes ( McKeon and Tracy, 2017 ). Our 
patient had an initial serum titer of 396 nmol/l and CSF titer of 4.79 
nmol/l ( Mayo Clinic Lab ). A recent series of three pediatric cases with 
positive anti-GAD-65 in both the serum and CSF manifested with auto -
immune encephalitis ( Ren et al., 2021 ). All three patients also had brain 
MRI and electroencephalogram (EEG) abnormalities. Interestingly, our 
patient did not present with encephalopathy or seizures despite high 
titers of anti-GAD-65 in both the serum and CSF. Her brain and spine 
MRIs were unremarkable as well. Therefore, we recommend autoim -
mune tests in patients presenting with MRI-negative myelopathy, to 
potentially resolve the diagnostic uncertainty. 
Up to now, our patient has responded well to combined treatments 
including clonazepam, IVIG, and physical therapy. We have followed 
serum anti-GAD-65 titers at several time points after IVIG had worn off 
( Table 1 ). While we did notice a titer rebound in serum GAD-65, TPO,

ANA antibodies after 2 months pause of IVIG treatment, the patient 
remained clinically stable. Our case has further illustrated that a high 
serum and/or CSF anti-GAD-65 titers does not necessarily correlate with 
the severity of clinical syndrome or treatment response. 
One study reported an estimated prevalence of 1 – 2 SMS/SPS cases 
per million in the UK general population, of which only 5% was seen in 
children ( Hadavi et al., 2011 ). Through an extensive literature review, 
we have identified 52 pediatric onset SMS/SPS or SLS that were previ -
ously published since 1980. These included the Johns Hopkins hospital 
cohort consisting 15 cases ( Yeshokumar et al., 2021 ) and the Mayo 
Clinic cohort of 8 cases ( Clardy et al., 2013 ), as well as single-case re -
ports ( Table 2 ). Including our own patient reported here, the clinical 
data of all 53 pediatric cases were analyzed. The sex distribution of re -
ported cases is 21 males (39.6%) to 32 females (60.4%). Age at symptom 
onset ranges from 0.25 to 17 years. Abnormally elevated serum and/or 
CSF anti-GAD-65 was documented in 32 cases. Additional 8 cases had 
concurrent anti-GAD-65 and GlyR antibodies. There were 3 cases posi -
tive for anti-GlyRa1 (Glycine receptor α 1 subunit) but negative anti- 
GAD-65. Therefore, positive anti-GAD-65 and/or anti-GlyR accounted 
for total 43 patients (81.1%). None of these patients have positive anti- 
amphiphysin or anti-gephyrin antibodies documented. The other 10 
patients (18.9%) were either negative or not tested for any of the anti -
bodies. T1DM and autoimmune thyroid diseases were the most common 
comorbid conditions and each found in 11 patients. Other concurrent 
autoimmune disorders included vitiligo ( N = 3), connective tissue dis -
orders ( N = 2), myasthenia gravis ( N = 1), Crohn ’ s disease (N = 1), 
rheumatoid arthritis (N = 1). Taken together, 56.6% of these patients ( N 
= 30) are associated with at least another autoimmune condition. 
Anxiety was diagnosed in 4 patients and epilepsia partialis continua 
(EPC) in one patient. However, it remains unclear as to what extent 
polyautoimmunity was present in these patients because in most reports, 
other autoantibodies were rarely tested or documented. The reported 
concurrent antiantibodies include TPO ( N = 3), thyroid thyrotropin 
receptor antibody ( N = 1), ANA (N = 3), anti-Insulin antibody ( N = 2), 
and anti-Islet cell antibody (N = 2). Nevertheless, our case has illus -
trated that a serology testing for other autoantibodies may offer a pre- 
symptomatic diagnosis of comorbidities in children presenting with 
SMS/SPS or SLS. 
As far as etiology goes, it remains largely unknown. Only 11 patients 
(21%) are associated with direct or indirect triggers such as an ante -
cedent infection. It was previously reported that approximately 4% of 
patients of all age groups with GAD-65 autoimmunity occurred in a 
paraneoplastic context ( McKeon et al., 2012 ). Coexisting anti- 
amphiphysin or anti-gephyrin or anti-GlyRa1 antibodies are more 
likely linked to paraneoplastic SMS/SPS ( McKeon et al., 2012 ; McKeon 
and Tracy, 2017 ; Folli et al., 1993 ; Butler et al., 2000 ). We found in this 
literature review that one patient had concurrent pleuropulmonary 
blastoma, but she tested negative for anti-GAD-65 and several other

advances in genetic testing in recent years will improve the diagnostic 
yield and accuracy. 
Immunotherapy and GABAergic agonists are mainstay treatments for 
SMS/SPS or SLS. Out of 53 pediatric cases, 46 patients (86.8%) received 
immunotherapy including IVIG, plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, Rit -
uximab, and others. Forty-three patients (81.1%) received symptomatic 
medications including benzodiazepines and/or Baclofen. Sixteen pa -
tients (30.2%) also received non-pharmacological treatments such as 
physical therapy, heat therapy, and others. The treatment response was 
classified as: 1) complete recovery, or mild symptoms with a modified 
Rankin Score (MRS) of 0 – 1 ( N = 15, 28.3%); 2) significant improvement 
but with residual physical deficits or MRS of 2 – 3 ( N = 35, 67.3%); 3) 
lack of response or worsening symptoms, or MRS of 4 – 5 ( N = 2, 3.8%). 
Therefore, the overall response rate was greater than 95%. There was 
one patient whose treatment response information was not ducumented. 
No deaths were reported. 
In summary, pediatric onset SMS/SPS or SLS are rare autoimmune 
conditions which can be associated with anti-GAD-65 and/or anti-GlyR, 
as well as other autoimmunities. Delay in diagnosis is not uncommon 
due to its rarity and often negative MRIs. Therefore, we should include 
SMS/SPS or SLS as an important differential diagnosis for MRI-negative 
myelopathy. The utilization of autoimmune panels and genetic testing 
will shorten the diagnostic odyssey in these patients and prevent a sig -
nificant delay in treatment initiation. Screening and surveillance for 
other autoimmune conditions are also warranted; however, paraneo -
plastic association is considered extremely rare in pediatric onset SMS/ 
SPS or SLS cases. While the majority of patients well respond to com -
bined immunotherapy, GABAergic agonists and supportive care, there 
will be continuing progression in symptom severity without prompt 
diagnosis and treatment initiation, and likely permanent physical defi -
cits in patients with treatment delay.

3. Case presentation 
An 18-month-old ex-full-term developmentally typical female with 
congenital first-degree AV block and tricuspid regurgitation presented to 
the emergency department (ED) due to inability to bear weight in her 
right lower extremity. Approximately 10 days prior to her hospital visit, 
her mother noted that she had a ‘wobbly gait ’ and a pain probably 
localized to her right hip that progressed over two days to no longer 
being able to ambulate and she preferred to crawl while dragging her leg 
behind her. There was no known trauma or injury. Parents endorsed a 
common cold approximately three weeks prior. She initially presented 
to an urgent care and then her pediatrician ’ s office where work-up 
included plain films of the right foot, fibula and tibia, all of which 
were normal. Laboratory data including a complete blood count, sedi -
mentation rate, C-reactive protein, Lyme titers and blood cultures were 
remarkable only for thrombocytosis to 659,000/mcl and leukocytosis to 
15,500/mcl. Symptoms continued to progress and the patient was 
referred back to the ED. On arrival , she was afebrile and hemody -
namically stable. Initially a musculoskeletal cause for her symptoms was 
pursued by the orthopedic team including repeat X-rays of the right 
tibia, fibula, femur, foot, pelvis and hips, all of which were normal. 
Repeat laboratory testing was also unremarkable aside from an elevated 
platelet count to 497,000/mcl; her leukocytosis had resolved. Magnetic 
resonance imaging (MRI) of the right hip and ankle was pursued and was 
normal. The patient was eventually discharged with possible diagnoses 
of transient synovitis or reactive arthritis of the hip or ankle. 
The patient presented again to the hospital 9 days later with 
continued functional decline. At that point she was unable to sit up 
without being assisted. Mother denied bowel or bladder dysfunction. On 
this admission neurology was consulted. Her initial neurologic exam 
was notable for rigidity, hypertonia and hyperreflexia on the right lower 
extremity compared to the left. Her interphalangeal (IP) joints of the big 
toes were in over-flexion. There was also reduced passive range of mo -
tion (ROM) in dorsiflexion and plantar flexion of both ankles, right more 
prominent than left. MRI of the entire neuro-axis was performed and was 
unremarkable. A lumbar puncture (LP) was pursued and the CSF routine

segments.text:
analysis was also normal (glucose 42, protein 17, RBCs 0 and nucleated 
cells 2). CSF neurotransmitters ( MNG lab ) and the gene panel for 
neurotransmitter disorders ( Invitae ) were sent and returned later as 
negative. Serum amino acids (SAA), urine organic acids (UOA) and CSF 
amino acids were unremarkable. She had also negative Lyme titer twice, 
normal creatinine kinase, acylcarnitine profile, serum copper and 
ceruloplasmin levels. At this point a search for more rare causes of MRI- 
negative myelopathy was pursued including both a serum and CSF 
screening for autoimmune myelopathy ( Mayo Clinic lab ). Notably, dur -
ing this time anti-ANA titers were abnormally elevated at 1:1,280 
(speckled). Anti-TPO antibodies were also elevated at 505 IU/ML and 
anti-islet cell antibodies elevated at 1,280 JDF units ( Table 1 ). There was 
consideration of empiric glucocorticoids treatment at that time. It was 
put on hold due to a worry for steroid-induced hyperglycemia, given her 
risk for T1DM, plus her symptoms began to slowly improve with 
intensive physical therapy. She was discharged with a close outpatient 
follow-up while awaiting autoimmune myelopathy panels to result. 
Soon after discharge the CSF autoimmune panel revealed an abnor -
mally elevated anti-GAD-65 antibodies at 4.79 nmol/l, with negative 
amphiphysin antibodies and negative NMO/AQP4 IgG levels. Serum 
anti-GAD-65 antibodies were remarkably elevated at 396 nmol/l (ref <
0.02 nmol/l) ( Table 1 ). This confirmed a diagnosis of SLS with positive 
anti-GAD-65 antibodies. Electromyography (EMG)/nerve conduction 
study was cancelled. She was subsequently started on a low dose of 
diazepam (2.5 mg by mouth three times a day) for spasticity and was 
then admitted for intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) treatment. Diaz -
epam was soon switched to clonazepam 0.25 mg by mouth twice daily 
after difficulty sleeping, decreased appetite, and loose stools were re -
ported as side-effects on diazepam. 
The patient continued to improve clinically over the next few weeks. 
She followed up with pediatric endocrinology and her linear growth was 
noted to be appropriate for her genetic potential. She had a work-up for 
endocrine conditions that included anti-insulin antibodies, insulin-like 
growth factor-1 (IGF-1), IGF binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3), cortisol, ad -
renocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), thyroid stimulating hormone 
(TSH), free T4, and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c). Her HbA1c was normal, 
ruling out T1DM, but her anti-insulin antibodies were positive, consis -
tent with the positive anti-GAD-65 and anti-islet cell antibodies and 
indicating an increased risk for developing T1DM. IGF-1 was low for age, 
IGFBP-3 was normal; cortisol and ACTH were normal, ruling out adrenal 
insufficiency, and TSH and free T4 were normal, consistent with 
euthyroid Hashimoto ’ s thyroiditis. Evaluation for other systemic auto -
immune diseases was pursued including anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, anti- 
RNP, anti-SSA, anti-SSB, and centromere B antibodies, anti-beta2 
glycoprotein IgG and IgM, anti-cardiolipin IgG, IgM, and IgA anti -
bodies, lupus anti-coagulant, tissue transglutaminase IgA, and results 
were all reassuring. A whole-body PET/CT (positron emission tomog -
raphy/computed tomography) scan showed no evidence of fluo -
rodeoxyglucose (FDG) avid malignancy. 
After receiving two treatments of monthly IVIG infusion (each 
treatment consisting of 1,000 mg/kg/day for two consecutive days), the

repeat serum anti-GAD-65 level was down-trending to 284. Given 
drastic clinical improvement, IVIG was temporally paused following the

segments.text:
3rd infusion. However, after a 2-month pause the titers of GAD-65, TPO 
and ANA antibodies had rebounded ( Table 1 ). Therefore, IVIG infusion 
had been resumed. Eight months after initial presentation, the patient 
developed autoimmune hypothyroidism and treatment with levothyr -
oxine was started. Patient followed with pediatric cardiology regularly 
and had stable cardiac status throughout the course. The Invitae primary 
immunodeficiency panel (407 genes) was non-diagnostic but revealed 
several heterozygous variants of unknown significance (VUS) in C2 
( c .259G > C; p. Val87Leu), CIITA ( c .2342C > G; p .Ser781Trp), NLRP12 
( c. 1790G > A; p. Ser597Asn), SAMD9L ( c. 982 T > C; p. Cys328Arg), and 
SRP72 ( c. 803A > G; p. Asn268Ser) genes. Of note, NLRP12, SAMD9L, 
and SRP72 genes are associated with autosomal dominant conditions, 
which are familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, ataxia- 
pancytopenia (AP) syndrome, and familial bone marrow failure, 
respectively. Parental study and whole exosome sequencing (WES) were 
recommended in a continued search for a genetic predisposition.
